title: Homeowner directly identifies themselves during registration
description: During account registration, the homeowner shares directly identifying data such as name, email address, phone number, postal address, or account credentials with the Home Hub. This makes the individual identifiable to the receiving system.
assumptions: Assumes registration requires personal account details rather than a fully anonymous/local-only setup.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-effort based on general LINDDUN identification taxonomy; exact sub-node may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Enrollment data can link the homeowner to specific devices and household context
description: By enrolling cameras and sensors on the Home Hub, the homeowner provides device identifiers, device types, room/location labels, and account association data that can be linked together to form a profile of the household and its owner.
assumptions: Assumes device enrollment includes persistent device IDs and/or user-assigned labels tied to the account.
uncertainty_note: Exact LINDDUN Pro sub-node may differ; threat applicability is strong even if the precise node label is approximate.

title: Data in transit may reveal the homeowner's identity or household identity
description: Registration and device-enrollment traffic may contain identifiers or metadata that reveal who is registering the system or which household the devices belong to if observed in transit.
assumptions: Assumes the flow traverses a network where traffic contents or metadata could be observed by intermediaries or local attackers.
uncertainty_note: Applies especially if transport protection or metadata minimization is weak; exact node is approximate.

title: Traffic metadata can link account creation with specific home devices
description: Even if payloads are protected, timing, endpoints, protocol metadata, and repeated enrollment exchanges can allow an observer to link a particular homeowner session to a set of cameras and sensors being enrolled.
assumptions: Assumes observable network metadata exists and device enrollment occurs over a networked channel.
uncertainty_note: Threat is plausible for network-visible enrollment flows; exact tree node is approximate.

title: Home Hub may collect more registration and device data than necessary
description: On receipt of registration and enrollment data, the Home Hub may request, infer, or store excessive personal and device information beyond what is necessary to create the account and pair cameras/sensors.
assumptions: Assumes the hub or its software supports optional fields, telemetry, rich device metadata, or broad default collection.
uncertainty_note: General detectability/disclosure distinction can vary by LINDDUN version; here this is treated as disclosure through over-collection at the destination.

title: Registration and enrollment data may be disclosed to unauthorized parties from the Home Hub
description: The Home Hub may expose stored account details, device identifiers, room labels, or household configuration to unauthorized local users, remote services, administrators, or attackers if access control, isolation, or secure storage is insufficient.
assumptions: Assumes the hub stores or forwards registration/enrollment data after receipt.
uncertainty_note: Exact sub-node is approximate, but disclosure risk at the destination is a strong fit.

title: The Home Hub may process registration and enrollment data without sufficient user awareness
description: If the Home Hub does not clearly explain what personal data and device metadata are collected, how long they are retained, whether they are shared with cloud services, or how enrollment affects monitoring, the homeowner may be unaware of the privacy impact of this flow.
assumptions: Assumes notices, setup UX, or consent prompts may be incomplete or unclear.
uncertainty_note: Exact node is approximate; threat depends on product UX and transparency design.

title: Registration and device enrollment may occur without valid or granular consent
description: The Home Hub may bundle account creation, device enrollment, telemetry, cloud synchronization, and analytics into a single acceptance step, preventing the homeowner from giving specific, informed, and freely given consent for each processing purpose.
assumptions: Assumes the product relies on consent or similar user permission for some processing activities.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on legal basis and product design; exact node is approximate.

title: Guest may be unaware they are sharing personal data when entering the temporary access code
description: By entering the temporary access code at the Home Hub, the guest shares data that can be associated with their visit or presence at the home. If the interface does not clearly explain what is collected, how long it is retained, or whether entry attempts are logged, the guest may be unaware of the privacy implications of providing the code.
assumptions: Assumes the temporary access code or associated event logs can be linked to a guest visit, time of presence, or identity by the system or homeowner.

title: Home Hub can detect a guest's presence and visit timing from code entry
description: When the Home Hub receives the temporary access code, it can infer that a guest is present at the door at a specific time and may associate the event with a particular temporary credential. This enables detection of the guest's arrival pattern or visit occurrence beyond the immediate purpose of unlocking the door.
assumptions: Assumes the Home Hub processes or stores successful or failed code-entry events with timestamps.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is given as a best-judgement generic detectability node because the retrieved context did not include the detailed detectability tree.

title: Home Hub may identify the guest through the temporary access code
description: If each temporary access code is unique to a specific guest or booking, the Home Hub can identify or single out which guest is attempting entry. This turns the code from a mere authenticator into an identifier of the individual or household visitor.
assumptions: Assumes temporary access codes are uniquely assigned or otherwise mappable to a specific guest record.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is approximate because the retrieved context did not include the detailed identifiability tree.

title: Home Hub may link this code entry to other guest activities
description: The Home Hub may link the received temporary access code and timestamp with other events such as prior entry attempts, door unlocks, camera events, booking records, or smart-home activity. This can create a richer profile of the guest's behavior and visits than is necessary for one-time access control.
assumptions: Assumes the Home Hub or connected systems maintain logs or correlated records across events and services.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is approximate because the retrieved context did not include the detailed linkability tree.

title: Guest may have no meaningful control over retention or further use of code-entry data
description: After receiving the temporary access code and related event data, the Home Hub may store or further use the information without offering the guest any way to access, correct, delete, or limit processing of those records. This creates non-compliance risk where privacy rights or data-minimization obligations apply.
assumptions: Assumes the Home Hub stores code-entry events or maps codes to guest-related records.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is approximate because the retrieved context did not include the detailed non-compliance tree.

title: Excessive collection of in-home sensor events into the log
description: The Home Hub may write more motion, door, and sensor-event data to the local event log than is necessary for the stated purpose. Because these events can reveal occupancy patterns, routines, and behavior inside the home, logging them by default or at overly fine granularity creates avoidable disclosure of personal data.
assumptions: Sensor events relate to identifiable household members or visitors, directly or by inference from household context.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort based on common LINDDUN Pro Dd decomposition around unnecessary collection/disclosure; exact subnode naming may vary by version.

title: Over-retention of detailed sensor history in the local event log
description: On receipt, the Local Event Log may store detailed motion, door, and sensor events longer than necessary. Retaining historical event streams enables reconstruction of presence, habits, sleep/work schedules, and other intimate household patterns, constituting avoidable disclosure through storage beyond need.
assumptions: The data store persists events for some period rather than acting as a transient buffer.
uncertainty_note: Exact Dd subnode id is approximate; threat applicability is strong, but the precise tree-node label may differ across LINDDUN Pro materials.

title: Linkability of sensor events into household behavior profiles
description: By accumulating multiple event types in one local log, the destination data store enables linking separate observations over time into a coherent profile of household routines and activities. Even if single events seem innocuous, their combination can link actions to the same home or person-pattern.
assumptions: Events are timestamped and associated with the same household/device context, allowing correlation over time.
uncertainty_note: Threat is well grounded; exact L subnode id is best-effort because the retrieved context did not include the detailed linkability tree.

title: Identifiability from persistent event records
description: Detailed local event records can make household members or regular visitors identifiable, directly or indirectly, through distinctive timing and activity patterns. For example, repeated door and motion sequences may single out a resident's schedule even without explicit names in the log.
assumptions: The household context or auxiliary knowledge exists such that behavior patterns can be tied to specific individuals.
uncertainty_note: Exact I subnode id is approximate; identifiability here is primarily indirect via behavioral patterns rather than explicit identifiers.

title: Detectability of occupancy and activity from presence of logged events
description: The existence, timing, and frequency of entries in the local event log can make private activities detectable. Even without reading full payloads, observing that events are being logged at certain times may reveal when someone is home, asleep, entering, or moving around.
assumptions: An observer or component can determine that log entries exist or can inspect metadata such as timestamps/counts.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort; the detectability threat itself is the main conclusion.

title: Insufficient user awareness that in-home events are being logged
description: If residents are not adequately informed that motion, door, and other sensor events are written to a persistent local log, they may be unaware of the extent of monitoring and storage. This undermines transparency about what personal data is processed and retained.
assumptions: The system may not clearly communicate local logging behavior, retention, or purpose to users.
uncertainty_note: Exact U subnode id is approximate; applicability depends on product transparency mechanisms not described in the flow.

title: Logging without valid consent or equivalent legal basis
description: Persistently storing detailed in-home sensor events in the local event log may require explicit consent or another valid legal basis, especially where the data reveals behavior inside the home. If the log is enabled by default or cannot be meaningfully controlled, non-compliance risk arises.
assumptions: Applicable law or policy requires consent or another lawful basis for this category of household monitoring data.
uncertainty_note: This is context-dependent on jurisdiction and deployment model; exact Nc subnode id is best-effort.

title: Uploading identifiable video clips discloses occupants and visitors to a third party
description: The Home Hub sends recorded camera clips to cloud storage. Video footage can directly reveal faces, bodies, behavior, home interiors, routines, and presence/absence patterns of residents and visitors. The act of transferring these clips from the home environment to a cloud provider increases disclosure of personal data to another party.
assumptions: Recorded clips contain personal data such as identifiable people, voices, timestamps, or contextual household details.
uncertainty_note: Threat-tree node id is based on best judgement; the exact sub-node may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Video content and transfer metadata may identify household members in transit
description: During upload, the clip payload and associated metadata such as device identifiers, account identifiers, timestamps, IP address, and camera/location labels can identify the household or specific individuals. Even if the main concern is the content itself, the data flow exposes identifying information while in transit.
assumptions: The upload includes metadata linking clips to a specific account, device, or household.
uncertainty_note: Exact node selection is approximate because the retrieved context did not include the detailed identification subtree.

title: Repeated clip uploads enable linkage of events and behavior over time
description: A sequence of uploads from the same Home Hub to the same cloud storage can be linked via persistent identifiers, network metadata, timestamps, and recurring visual context. This allows correlation of multiple clips into a profile of household routines, occupancy, visitors, and activities.
assumptions: Uploads use stable account, device, or network identifiers that permit correlation across sessions.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is based on best judgement; linkage clearly applies, but the precise subtree reference may differ.

title: Cloud storage may expose highly sensitive household footage
description: Once received by Cloud Video Storage, the provider can store and make the clips accessible to internal systems, administrators, subprocessors, or other services. Centralized retention of home camera footage increases the risk of disclosure of intimate household activities, visitors, and security-relevant events.
assumptions: Cloud storage personnel or connected services may have logical access to stored clips or derived metadata.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate; the disclosure risk at the destination is clear.

title: Stored camera clips may be retained longer than necessary
description: Cloud Video Storage may keep uploaded clips beyond the period needed for the stated purpose, violating the storage limitation principle. Extended retention of home surveillance footage increases privacy impact because old clips continue to reveal household behavior and visitors.
assumptions: Retention periods are not strictly limited, enforced, or communicated to users.

title: Secondary use of uploaded clips may exceed the original home-security purpose
description: After receipt, the cloud provider may analyze or reuse stored clips for purposes beyond user-expected video backup or security monitoring, such as service improvement, model training, analytics, or law-enforcement response workflows. Such downstream use can be incompatible with the original purpose for collection.
assumptions: Provider terms, backend analytics, or integrations permit processing beyond simple storage and retrieval.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is based on best judgement because no unlinkability subtree was provided in context.

title: Insufficient evidence of upload, access, or deletion can undermine accountability
description: If Cloud Video Storage does not maintain reliable logs or receipts for clip upload, access, sharing, and deletion events, the provider or user may later be unable to prove what happened to specific footage. This creates repudiation risk around whether clips were uploaded, viewed, shared, or erased.
assumptions: Audit trails, tamper-evident logs, or user-visible histories may be incomplete or absent.
uncertainty_note: Repudiation applicability is plausible for this flow, but depends on whether accountability and logging are in scope for the modeled system.

title: Home Hub may disclose more motion-alert data than necessary to the backend
description: When forwarding a real-time motion alert, the Home Hub may include avoidable personal data beyond what is strictly needed for alert handling, such as precise timestamps, device identifiers, household identifiers, sensor metadata, or repeated event details. Because motion events reveal occupancy and behavior patterns, oversharing from P1 to P2 creates an explicit data-disclosure risk.
assumptions: Assumes the alert payload can contain metadata beyond the minimum needed to notify and route the event.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement for unnecessary/overly detailed disclosure; retrieved context did not provide the exact Dd subtree mapping.

title: Real-time motion alerts in transit can identify the household or user
description: Even if the payload is limited, data in transit may contain identifiers or quasi-identifiers such as account IDs, hub IDs, IP-address-related metadata, routing headers, or stable tokens that allow the receiving side or intermediaries to identify a specific household or resident. A motion alert is strongly tied to a home context and can therefore become identifying when combined with transport metadata.
assumptions: Assumes network- or application-layer metadata is visible to parties handling the transmission and that identifiers are stable across events.
uncertainty_note: Exact I subtree node is approximate; threat applicability depends on protocol and identifier design.

title: Repeated motion alerts can be linked into occupancy and behavior profiles
description: Because the flow carries recurring real-time motion events from the same hub to the backend, stable identifiers, timing patterns, and source metadata can allow events to be linked together. This enables reconstruction of routines such as presence at home, sleep/wake cycles, and periods of absence, even if each individual alert appears limited.
assumptions: Assumes alerts are associated with a persistent hub/account/session identifier or otherwise correlate through timing and network metadata.
uncertainty_note: Exact L subtree node is approximate; linkage may occur through payload, metadata, or both.

title: Backend receipt of motion alerts enables detection of residents' activities and presence
description: By receiving and processing real-time motion alerts, the mobile app backend can infer whether someone is at home, when movement occurs, and potentially daily routines or unusual events. This creates a detectability threat because the backend can observe the occurrence of privacy-relevant events about the household.
assumptions: Assumes P2 processes or logs incoming alerts rather than acting as a blind relay.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; retrieved context did not include the D threat tree.

title: Backend may retain or further share motion-alert data beyond the immediate notification purpose
description: Once the backend receives the motion alert, it may store, replicate, analyze, or expose the event to additional internal services, operators, analytics systems, or third parties beyond what is necessary to deliver the mobile notification. This constitutes avoidable downstream disclosure of sensitive in-home activity data.
assumptions: Assumes P2 persists alerts or forwards them to other components/services.
uncertainty_note: Exact Dd subtree node is approximate; threat depends on backend architecture and data-sharing practices.

title: Backend-side processing of motion alerts may be insufficiently transparent to residents
description: Residents may not understand that real-time motion alerts sent from the Home Hub are received by the backend, potentially logged, analyzed for service improvement, or used for operational monitoring. If these purposes, recipients, or retention periods are not made clear, the flow contributes to an unawareness threat.
assumptions: Assumes user-facing notices may not fully explain backend handling of motion-event data.
uncertainty_note: Exact U subtree node is approximate; this depends on the quality of privacy notices and in-app explanations.

title: Backend processing of motion alerts may exceed or conflict with the user's consent or expected purpose
description: If users consent only to security notifications, but the backend also uses motion alerts for analytics, profiling, feature training, or broader monitoring, the destination processing may not align with the granted consent or expected purpose limitation. This creates a non-compliance risk for the flow.
assumptions: Assumes consent, contract terms, or regulatory basis may be narrower than actual backend uses.
uncertainty_note: Exact Nc subtree node is approximate; applicability depends on the stated legal basis, consent scope, and jurisdiction.

title: Notification reveals more personal data than necessary
description: The backend may include excessive detail in the motion alert sent to the homeowner, such as exact timestamps, camera/location identifiers, thumbnails, or inferred occupancy information, when a less detailed alert would suffice. This creates avoidable disclosure of personal data across the system boundary.
assumptions: The notification content may contain event details beyond a minimal 'motion detected' message.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selected by best judgement based on data-minimisation/explicit disclosure; exact node id may vary by LINDDUN Pro version.

title: Push-notification metadata discloses behavioral information in transit
description: Even if the payload is minimal, metadata on the notification flow—such as recipient identity, delivery timing, frequency of alerts, and association with a specific home-security app—can reveal occupancy patterns, routines, or that motion events occurred at the homeowner's residence.
assumptions: Notification delivery involves observable metadata at transport or intermediary push-service layers.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree node id for implicit/metadata disclosure is approximate.

title: Notification content may be exposed on the homeowner device
description: On receipt, the notification may appear on the lock screen, notification shade, wearable, or shared device, allowing other nearby people to learn that motion was detected at the homeowner's property and infer presence/absence or security status.
assumptions: The homeowner device may display notifications visibly before device unlock or may be accessible to others.
uncertainty_note: Destination-side disclosure is clear, but the exact node id is chosen by best judgement.

title: Repeated alerts can link events to a specific homeowner or household
description: The pattern and routing metadata of motion notifications can enable linking multiple motion events to the same recipient, household, or property over time, building a profile of the homeowner's routines and home activity.
assumptions: An observer or intermediary can correlate repeated notifications by recipient, device token, account, or app channel.
uncertainty_note: Applicable linkability threat is plausible for push-notification metadata; exact node id is approximate.

title: Notification metadata may identify the homeowner
description: Identifiers used to route the push notification, such as device tokens, account identifiers, or app-specific addressing information, may directly or indirectly identify the homeowner to intermediaries handling the notification.
assumptions: Push delivery uses stable identifiers visible to service providers or network intermediaries.
uncertainty_note: Identification risk depends on what routing identifiers are exposed to intermediaries.

title: Homeowner may be unaware of notification visibility and downstream exposure
description: The homeowner may not understand that motion alerts can be shown on lock screens, mirrored to wearables, or exposed through device notification settings, reducing their ability to make informed choices about receiving such alerts.
assumptions: The system does not clearly explain notification-display behavior or privacy-relevant settings.
uncertainty_note: This is a usability/unawareness threat contingent on product UX rather than the flow alone.

title: Backend may send motion alerts without sufficiently specific consent or preference control
description: If the backend pushes motion-detected notifications without the homeowner having explicitly enabled this category of alert, chosen its level of detail, or being able to withdraw that choice, the disclosure may occur without valid consent or user control.
assumptions: Notification preferences and consent granularity may be absent or insufficiently specific.
uncertainty_note: Consent applicability depends on the legal basis and product design; included because notification categories often require user choice.

title: Sharing analytics may enable cross-context linkage by the vendor
description: When the mobile app backend sends aggregated device-usage analytics to the cloud analytics vendor, stable cohort keys, device characteristics, app/version fields, timestamps, or campaign identifiers in the payload can allow the vendor to link this dataset with other datasets it already holds, correlating the same users, devices, or cohorts across customers or services.
assumptions: Applies if the 'aggregated' analytics still contains persistent identifiers, quasi-identifiers, fine-grained dimensions, or repeated cohort labels that remain stable over time.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-judgement because the retrieved context provided applicable threat types/positions but not the detailed subtree for linkability.

title: In-transit analytics metadata may identify the app operator or user segments
description: Even if payload contents are aggregated, the data flow itself can expose identifying information through endpoint metadata, request headers, tenant identifiers, API keys, IP addresses, timing, or payload structure. This may identify the sending service and potentially reveal which product, region, or user segment the analytics concerns.
assumptions: Applies if transport- or application-layer metadata is observable by intermediaries or the vendor beyond what is strictly necessary.
uncertainty_note: Identification of individual end users from this flow is less certain because the description says 'aggregated' analytics; this threat is stronger for identification of the sender or cohorts than for direct user identification.

title: Vendor may infer sensitive or behavioral information from aggregated usage analytics
description: On receipt, the cloud analytics vendor can analyze aggregated device-usage patterns to derive additional knowledge about user populations, behaviors, locations, health-related app usage, or other sensitive traits, especially when combined with other datasets or benchmarks. Such derivation can exceed what data subjects reasonably expect from the original collection context.
assumptions: Applies if the aggregates are sufficiently granular by time, geography, feature, device type, or cohort to support meaningful inference.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is approximate; the exact derivation subtree may differ in the formal catalog.

title: Secondary analytics use by the vendor may exceed the original purpose
description: The cloud analytics vendor may use the received analytics not only to provide contracted analytics services, but also for product improvement, benchmarking across customers, model training, fraud detection, or other secondary purposes that are not aligned with the original purpose for which the mobile app backend collected the data.
assumptions: Applies unless contractual and technical controls strictly limit the vendor to processor-only use for the specified analytics purpose.
uncertainty_note: This is a common purpose-limitation risk for third-party analytics sharing; exact subtree id is best-judgement.

title: Sharing aggregated analytics with a third-party vendor may occur without adequate transparency or legal basis
description: If users were not clearly informed that their device-usage analytics would be disclosed to an external cloud analytics vendor, or if the aggregation level does not remove the data from privacy-law scope, the disclosure and subsequent processing may violate consent, transparency, processor-controller allocation, cross-border transfer, or data-minimization obligations.
assumptions: Applies if notices, consent mechanisms, data-processing agreements, transfer safeguards, or lawful-basis assessments are missing or insufficient.
uncertainty_note: Compliance applicability depends on jurisdiction and whether the shared analytics is truly anonymized; exact subtree id is approximate.

title: Linkability via retrieval metadata on the video-fetch flow
description: Metadata on this retrieval flow (e.g., clip identifier, homeowner/account identifier, device/app identifier, timestamps, IP address, and repeated access patterns) could allow an observer of the flow or intermediary logs to link multiple video accesses to the same homeowner, household, or camera over time.
assumptions: Assumes the flow or supporting infrastructure exposes stable identifiers or observable metadata beyond what is strictly necessary, and that such metadata is accessible to network intermediaries or logging systems.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node citation is based on best judgment because the retrieved context did not include the specific Linkability subtree for DataStore->Process flows.

title: Identifiability of homeowner through video retrieval traffic
description: The retrieval request/response may contain or reveal identifiers that directly or indirectly identify the homeowner or household, such as account IDs, camera IDs, signed URLs, network addresses, or timing/location patterns associated with playback of a specific stored clip.
assumptions: Assumes identifiers or distinctive metadata are present in the flow or adjacent transport/logging layers.
uncertainty_note: Specific Identifiability tree-node citation is approximate; the exact subtree was not provided in the retrieved context.

title: Disclosure of sensitive video content in transit
description: The stored video clip and associated metadata may be exposed during transfer from cloud storage to the backend if transport protection, access scoping, or intermediary handling is insufficient. Video footage from a home environment can reveal highly sensitive personal data about residents, visitors, routines, and possessions.
assumptions: Assumes the clip or metadata could be observed by unauthorized parties in transit or via intermediary components such as proxies, caches, or logs.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node citation is based on general LINDDUN disclosure-in-transit reasoning; exact subtree id may differ.

title: Excessive retention or secondary exposure of retrieved video at the backend
description: Once P2 retrieves the clip, the backend may temporarily store, cache, duplicate, or log the video or its metadata in ways that expose it to unauthorized internal access or broaden its availability beyond the immediate playback purpose.
assumptions: Assumes P2 performs caching, buffering, debugging, analytics, or operational logging of retrieved content or metadata.
uncertainty_note: Exact Disclosure subtree id is approximate because the retrieved context did not include the relevant D threat tree.

title: Use of retrieved video beyond the homeowner playback purpose
description: The backend could process the retrieved clip or its metadata for purposes beyond serving playback, such as analytics, model training, employee review, profiling, or service improvement, without necessity or user expectation.
assumptions: Assumes governance or technical controls do not strictly bind P2 to the playback purpose.
uncertainty_note: Purpose-limitation / policy non-conformance subtree id is based on best judgment; exact U node may differ.

title: Violation of storage limitation for retrieved video copies at the backend
description: P2 may retain fetched video clips, thumbnails, buffers, or related access records longer than necessary for playback, violating storage-limitation obligations.
assumptions: Assumes the backend creates persistent or semi-persistent copies/logs during retrieval handling.
